teaser: Looking at Medusa turns you to stone. This Perseus looks straight at her.
review_notes:
The Met version is the second, carved about 1804-06 for Countess Valeria Tarnowska of Poland; the first (1797-1801) was bought by Pope Pius VII for the Vatican. Met acquired it in 1967.
Canova named Inspector General of Antiquities and Fine Arts for the Papal States in 1802; called to Paris by Napoleon in 1802; declined to settle there.
Colossal nude Napoleon as Mars the Peacemaker completed 1806; Paolina Borghese as Venus begun about 1805.
First Perseus placed on the Vatican pedestal left empty by the Apollo Belvedere, taken to Paris in 1797-98 and returned in 1816.
Canova's ribs deformed by years of pressing a running drill against his chest: reported by his early biographers, please verify.
Medusa's face modeled on the ancient Rondanini Medusa (then in Rome, now Munich): standard account.
Height about 242 cm.
The sandals in this photo show straps and ankle ornaments; the lesson does not claim visible wings on them.

lesson.text: Around 1806 Antonio Canova was 48, single, rich and worn out. He was the most wanted sculptor in Europe. Napoleon had called him to Paris and pressed him to stay. He said no and went home to Rome, where he was finishing a nude marble Napoleon over three meters tall and a portrait of the emperor's sister lying on a couch.

He also held a public job. Since 1802 he had been the pope's Inspector General of Fine Arts, in charge of stopping Rome's treasures from leaving. That job explains why the statue in this photo exists. It is a second version, and the first one was caught by exactly the kind of rule Canova now enforced.

The first Perseus, finished in 1801, was about to be sold out of Rome when the pope stepped in and bought it for the Vatican. A Polish countess, Valeria Tarnowska, still wanted one. So Canova carved the figure again for her, adjusting details as he went. That replica, 2.4 meters tall (nearly 8 feet), is the one now in New York.

The pope gave the first Perseus a very particular spot: the empty pedestal of the Apollo Belvedere, the most admired ancient statue in the Vatican, which French troops had carried off to Paris. A living sculptor was being asked to fill the place of the ancients.

The myth is Greek. Medusa is a monster with snakes for hair, and anyone who meets her eyes turns to stone. The young hero Perseus is sent to bring back her head. The gods lend him equipment: a cap that makes him invisible, winged footwear, a polished shield to use as a mirror, and a special blade.
The weapon in his hand is not an ordinary sword. Tap the part that makes it different.

spots.title: The hook
spots.text: A curved spur juts from the back of the blade. This is the harpe, the hooked sword that Greek artists gave to Perseus. Canova copied it from ancient images, as he did the winged cap.

lesson.text: Canova was a careful reader of ancient art, and that hook is a quotation. But he took one large liberty with the story. In the myth, Perseus never looks at Medusa. He strikes while watching her reflection, then stuffs the head in a bag. Follow the direction of this Perseus's eyes.
The statue is built on a few clear directions, almost like a drawing.

lines.label: The forbidden look
lines.text: He gazes directly at the severed head, calm and curious. By the rules of the myth he should now turn to stone. And of course he has: he is marble.

lines.label: The trophy arm
lines.text: The arm stretches out level from the shoulder and holds the head by its hair, away from the body. It is displayed to him and to us at once.

lines.label: A slow step
lines.text: The weight rests on the front leg while the other trails behind, toes barely down. He is walking away from the deed, unhurried. The fight is over.

lines.label: The cloak
lines.text: Cloth falls from the raised arm to the ground behind the legs. It looks casual. It is also engineering: a hidden bridge of marble that helps the ankles carry the statue.

lesson.text: Canova shows the moment after violence, when it has already turned into stillness. That choice of calm over action is the heart of Neoclassicism.

Neoclassicism was the style of his generation: a return to the clean outlines and quiet poses of Greek and Roman statues, after a century of swirling, emotional Baroque art. Compare the most famous earlier Perseus, a bronze in Florence from the 1500s: blood pours from the neck and the body lies crushed under the hero's feet. Canova's version has no blood, no corpse, no sweat.

Medusa's face is a portrait of another sculpture. Canova based it on an ancient marble mask then famous in Rome, the Rondanini Medusa, which shows her not as a monster but as a beautiful woman with small wings in her hair and a look of sorrow.

Her head rewards a long look: snakes knotted under the chin, mouth open, brows drawn together as if in pain. She is the only one in the statue who seems to feel anything. Perseus, smooth and blank, studies her like a visitor in a gallery. Some viewers have always found him a little cold.

Such smoothness cost him physically. Canova spent decades leaning his chest against a hand drill to bore into marble, and his biographers report that the pressure slowly pushed in his ribs and troubled his stomach for the rest of his life.

The countess's Perseus stayed in private hands for a century and a half, until the Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1967. It stands there today in the pose you see. Which leaves a question the myth cannot answer: is he looking at a monster, or at the first thing he has ever killed?

quiz.question: Why did Canova carve this second Perseus?
options: The first one broke in transport
The pope kept the first in Rome, and a Polish countess wanted one
Napoleon ordered a copy for Paris
quiz.explanation: The first was bought for the Vatican, so Countess Tarnowska received a second version.

quiz.question: What is special about the sword Perseus holds?
options: It has a hook on the blade
It is carved from a different stone
quiz.explanation: It is the harpe, the hooked sword of Greek images of Perseus.

quiz.question: How does Canova's hero break the rule of the myth?
options: He looks straight at Medusa's face
He holds the head in his left hand
quiz.explanation: In the story he only looks at her reflection, but here he gazes at her directly.

quiz.question: What practical job does the hanging cloak do?
options: It hides a crack in the marble
It helps support the statue's weight
quiz.explanation: The marble cloth links the arm to the ground and relieves the ankles.

quiz.question: What did Canova use as the model for Medusa's face?
options: An ancient marble mask of Medusa in Rome
quiz.explanation: He based it on the Rondanini Medusa, an ancient sculpture.

facts.text: Canova moved to Paris to work for Napoleon.
facts.explanation: He was invited but refused and returned to Rome.

facts.text: The first Perseus was placed on the pedestal of the missing Apollo Belvedere.
facts.explanation: The pope set it where the ancient statue had stood before the French took it.

facts.text: Canova shows blood pouring from Medusa's neck.
facts.explanation: His version is clean and calm, with no blood or body.
